note: v0.25: principles translated into tests on monthly US data since 1871; tested by buildout/reason.py.

rules.principle: A calm market does not mean low tail risk, so crash risk after low volatility is not lower than after high volatility.
rules.source_title: The Fourth Quadrant: A Map of the Limits of Statistics (Edge, Sep 14, 2008)
rules.quote: Do not confuse absence of volatility with absence of risks.
rules.vs: the same months without the condition
rules.note: Direct test of the claim; volatility clustering predicts the opposite, so this rule is likely to fail and its failure size is the informative part.
rules.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Quote verbatim; principle is a fair reading and the note explains the test.

rules.principle: Worst drawdowns after quiet periods are as deep as after turbulent ones because tail risk accumulates in calm.
rules.source_title: The Fourth Quadrant: A Map of the Limits of Statistics (Edge, Sep 14, 2008)
rules.quote: Do not confuse absence of volatility with absence of risks.
rules.vs: the same months without the condition
rules.note: maxdd12 is negative, so lower means deeper; the honest reading is that Taleb predicts no improvement, a strictly deeper drawdown is the strong version and likely fails.
rules.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Quote verbatim; accumulation-in-calm wording goes past the page but the note frames it as the strong version.

rules.principle: Calm combined with prices far above trend is the fragile configuration in which a shock does the most damage.
rules.source_title: The Fourth Quadrant: A Map of the Limits of Statistics (Edge, Sep 14, 2008)
rules.quote: Do not confuse absence of volatility with absence of risks.
rules.vs: the same months without the condition
rules.note: Loose translation joining the low-volatility warning with distance above trend; thresholds are round numbers, not fitted.
rules.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Quote verbatim; note flags the loose translation.

rules.principle: High valuations after an era of easy money make the market fragile, so the worst drawdown ahead is deeper.
rules.source_title: 'Disneyland is over': 'The Black Swan' author says the easy money era is over and compares Bitcoin to a 'tumor' (Fortune, Feb 1, 2023)
rules.quote: All these years, assets were inflating like crazy
rules.vs: the same months without the condition
rules.note: Uses CAPE percentile as the measurable stand-in for asset inflation; lower maxdd12 means a deeper fall.
rules.checked: corrected by a second checker: Quote verbatim; easy-money asset inflation supports a loose fragility reading as the note says; headline differs.

rules.principle: Low rates that inflated assets leave expensive markets exposed to large drawdowns.
rules.source_title: 'Disneyland is over': 'The Black Swan' author says the easy money era is over and compares Bitcoin to a 'tumor' (Fortune, Feb 1, 2023)
rules.quote: It's not going to be as smooth as it was the last 15 years.
rules.vs: the same months without the condition
rules.note: Translates the free-money argument into low yields plus high valuation; few pre-2000 months qualify, so the sample is thin.
rules.checked: corrected by a second checker: Quote verbatim; article ties zero rates to inflated assets; note flags the translation; headline differs.

rules.principle: Past Black Swans do not predict future ones, so a recent large drawdown should not change crash odds.
rules.source_title: The Fourth Quadrant: A Map of the Limits of Statistics (Edge, Sep 14, 2008)
rules.quote: past Black Swans do not predict future Black Swans
rules.vs: the same months without the condition
rules.note: Taleb predicts no difference; the rule is stated as higher so that a significant result in either direction counts against his claim.
rules.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Quote verbatim (40 years of data sentence); note explains the null-hypothesis framing.

rules.principle: After a sharp selloff in an expensive market, a further fall two or three times larger is in line with fat tails.
rules.source_title: The Black Swan author warns future selloffs could be 2-3 times worse than DeepSeek shock (Fortune, Feb 2, 2025)
rules.quote: or two three times bigger even
rules.vs: the same months without the condition
rules.note: Uses a 10% real drawdown from peak with high CAPE as the analog of the Jan 2025 shock; loose.
rules.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Quote verbatim; page has no valuation angle but the note flags the CAPE analog as loose.

rules.principle: Tail risk is structurally underpriced during strong rallies, so crashes are more likely after big momentum.
rules.source_title: Black Swan author warns investors (TheStreet via Yahoo Finance, Feb 25, 2026)
rules.quote: Tail-risk across sectors is structurally underpriced.
rules.vs: the same months without the condition
rules.note: No option prices exist back to 1871, so underpricing is proxied by a strong trailing rally; momentum evidence makes failure likely.
rules.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Quote verbatim; note flags momentum as a proxy for underpricing.

rules.principle: Investors who avoid ruin and stay in the game capture the rebound after deep drawdowns.
rules.source_title: The Logic of Risk Taking (Taleb, Incerto on Medium)
rules.quote: no person can get the returns of the market unless he has infinite pockets and no uncle points.
rules.vs: the same months without the condition
rules.note: Tests the cost of an uncle point: if returns after deep drawdowns are higher, forced exits there destroy wealth.
rules.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Quote verbatim; staying in the game is the page's point and the note explains the test.

rules.principle: Expensive markets can rise much further in a euphoric blow-off before the crash.
rules.source_title: US stocks may surge another 20% before historic crash, says Black Swan fund (Reuters via Kitco, Sep 23, 2025)
rules.quote: only after a massive, euphoric, historic blow off rally
rules.vs: the same months without the condition
rules.note: Tests the blow-off half of the thesis: high valuation plus strong momentum should still earn above-average next-year returns.
rules.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Quote verbatim; blow-off-then-crash thesis supports the higher ret12 test.

rules.principle: The largest bubbles end in crashes, so the most expensive markets have lower forward returns.
rules.source_title: Black Swan investor sees 'euphoric high' ahead, then an 80% crash (Fortune, Apr 1, 2025)
rules.quote: the largest bubble in human history popping
rules.vs: the same months without the condition
rules.note: Uses the top 5% of CAPE history as the bubble state; 12-month horizon is short for a valuation signal.
rules.checked: corrected by a second checker: Quote verbatim; note flags the short horizon; headline differs.

rules.principle: Easing into an expensive market precedes the hard landing and crash.
rules.source_title: Black Swan investor sees 'euphoric high' ahead, then an 80% crash (Fortune, Apr 1, 2025)
rules.quote: hard landing, panicking Fed. And that's a crash.
rules.vs: the same months without the condition
rules.note: Loose: a fall of more than 100 bp in the 10-year yield over 12 months proxies Fed easing; the policy rate is not in the variable set.
rules.checked: corrected by a second checker: Quote verbatim; page has easing then panicking Fed then crash, note flags the proxy; headline differs.

rules.principle: Volatility is not a stable quantity under fat tails, so quiet years are followed by more volatility than they show.
rules.source_title: The Fourth Quadrant: A Map of the Limits of Statistics (Edge, Sep 14, 2008)
rules.quote: Words like "standard deviation" are not stable
rules.vs: the same months without the condition
rules.note: Compared with the complement this almost surely fails, since volatility persists; it is kept to measure how strongly calm persists against Taleb's instability claim.
rules.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Quote verbatim; note concedes the translation is a stretch test.

rules.principle: Fast earnings growth at high valuations reflects optimization without redundancy and precedes deeper drawdowns.
rules.source_title: The Fourth Quadrant: A Map of the Limits of Statistics (Edge, Sep 14, 2008)
rules.quote: Avoid Optimization, Learn to Love Redundancy.
rules.vs: the same months without the condition
rules.note: Loose translation of over-optimization into an earnings boom at high valuation; likely to fail if earnings momentum dominates.
rules.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Quote verbatim; note flags the loose translation.

rules.principle: Get out of anything that falls below its 200-day moving average, because downtrends carry the large losses.
rules.source_title: 25iq, A Dozen Things I've Learned from Paul Tudor Jones
rules.quote: get out of anything that falls below the 200-day moving average
rules.note: The 200-day daily average is translated to the 10-month average of monthly prices (about 210 trading days); maxdd12 lower means a deeper worst drawdown ahead.
rules.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Quote verbatim on 25iq; 10-month translation of the 200-day rule is fair and disclosed.

rules.principle: Below the 200-day average the odds of a large fall are higher, so defense comes first.
rules.source_title: 25iq, A Dozen Things I've Learned from Paul Tudor Jones
rules.quote: My guiding philosophy is playing great defense.
rules.note: Same 10-month translation of the 200-day rule, tested on the crash indicator rather than return; a fair test of the defensive claim.
rules.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Quote verbatim on 25iq ('My guiding philosophy is playing great defense.'); fair translation.

rules.principle: Prices move along the line of least resistance, so the next move tends to continue the current trend.
rules.source_title: Advisor Perspectives, Jesse Livermore (Feb 27, 2017)
rules.quote: Prices, like everything else, move along the line of least resistance.
rules.note: Livermore traded swings of weeks to months; a one-month return after price above trend and positive 12-month momentum is a fair but coarse analog.
rules.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Quote verbatim on Advisor Perspectives; coarse monthly analog disclosed in note.

rules.principle: The big money is made by sitting tight through the main movement, not trading the fluctuations.
rules.source_title: Edwin Lefevre, Reminiscences of a Stock Operator (1923)
rules.quote: It was always my sitting.
rules.note: A strong 12-month advance stands for an established main movement; a 12-month holding outcome tests whether sitting tight pays at index level.
rules.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Quote verbatim in Gutenberg text; principle matches the main-movements passage.

rules.principle: Never average losses: adding to a market that is falling and below trend loses money.
rules.source_title: Kitco, Jesse Livermore, world's greatest trader (May 2, 2023)
rules.quote: Never average losses.
rules.note: Loose: the rule concerns adding to one's own losing trade; here it is read as buying the index while it is in a confirmed decline.
rules.checked: confirmed by a second checker: 'Never average losses.' verbatim on Kitco; loose index reading disclosed.

rules.principle: The time of maximum pessimism is the best time to buy.
rules.source_title: Lauren Templeton, Ivey Business School presentation (2012)
rules.quote: The time of maximum pessimism is the best time to buy
rules.note: A real drawdown beyond 30% from the prior peak is a price-based proxy for maximum pessimism; no sentiment series exists since 1871.
rules.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Quote verbatim in 2012 Templeton deck; price proxy for pessimism disclosed.

rules.principle: Bull markets die on euphoria, so very rich valuations after a strong run precede weak returns.
rules.source_title: Lauren Templeton, Ivey Business School presentation (2012)
rules.quote: mature on optimism and die on euphoria
rules.note: Top-5% valuation plus a 15% momentum run is a proxy for euphoria; loose because euphoria is a sentiment state, not a price state.
rules.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Quote verbatim in 2012 deck; looseness disclosed.

rules.principle: In the acceleration phase of a boom the trend is reinforced by expectations, so riding it pays until the moment of truth.
rules.source_title: George Soros, Fallibility, Reflexivity, and the Human Uncertainty Principle
rules.quote: the trend is recognized and reinforced by expectations
rules.note: High valuation with positive momentum marks a boom; the short ret1 horizon tests riding it, which differs from the valuation view that returns are low over 12 months.
rules.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Quote verbatim on georgesoros.com; translation fair and explained.

rules.principle: Booms are slow and busts abrupt, so a rich market whose trend has turned down faces elevated crash risk.
rules.source_title: George Soros, Fallibility, Reflexivity, and the Human Uncertainty Principle
rules.quote: busts tend to be more abrupt
rules.note: Rich valuation plus a broken 10-month trend approximates the twilight period and crossover point; a fair translation of the shape, not of the full sequence.
rules.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Quote verbatim on georgesoros.com; fair translation of the shape.

rules.principle: Liquidity, not earnings, moves the overall market, so tightening conditions hurt forward returns.
rules.source_title: Livewire, Stanley Druckenmiller: The two things my mentor taught me (Apr 14, 2015)
rules.quote: It's liquidity that moves markets.
rules.note: Loose: a 100bp rise in the 10-year yield over 12 months stands in for Fed tightening and draining liquidity; no policy-rate or balance-sheet series exists since 1871.
rules.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Quote verbatim on Livewire; yield proxy disclosed as loose.

rules.principle: Earnings do not move the overall market, so strong trailing earnings growth should not predict higher index returns.
rules.source_title: Livewire, Stanley Druckenmiller: The two things my mentor taught me (Apr 14, 2015)
rules.quote: Earnings don't move the overall market.
rules.note: This encodes the conventional view Druckenmiller rejects; if he is right the rule should FAIL the evidence gate.
rules.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Quote verbatim on Livewire; contra framing clearly disclosed.

rules.principle: Never invest in the present: buy when current earnings are poor but the trajectory is improving.
rules.source_title: Livewire, Stanley Druckenmiller: The two things my mentor taught me (Apr 14, 2015)
rules.quote: Never, ever invest in the present.
rules.note: Negative but accelerating earnings growth proxies for a world that will look better in 18 months; loose because his view is mostly about liquidity and policy.
rules.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Quote verbatim on Livewire; looseness disclosed.

rules.principle: Real bottoms end at 10- or 15-year lows, so the cheapest valuations in history mark the best entry points.
rules.source_title: Moomoo Learn, Jim Rogers: Invest only in what you have knowledge about
rules.quote: they end with 10- or 15-year lows
rules.note: Loose: a bottom-decile CAPE percentile stands in for multi-year lows, since no 10-year price low variable is given.
rules.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Quote fragment verbatim on Moomoo ('they end with 10- or 15-year lows'); CAPE proxy disclosed as loose.

rules.principle: Do not try to buy at the bottom: a deep decline that is still falling keeps falling in the near term.
rules.source_title: 25iq, A Dozen Things I've Learned from Bernard Baruch about Investing
rules.quote: Don't try to buy at the bottom and sell at the top.
rules.note: Loose: Baruch warns that exact bottoms cannot be timed, not that falling markets keep falling; this tests the near-term cost of buying a falling 20%-plus drawdown and competes directly with the Templeton maximum-pessimism rule.
rules.checked: corrected by a second checker: Quote verbatim on 25iq, but Baruch warns against timing exact turns; reading it as a forecast that deep falling drawdowns keep falling is loose and the note did not say so.

rules.principle: When price and earnings take a back seat to momentum, step aside because the eventual drawdown is large.
rules.source_title: A Letter a Day, Letter #78: Julian Robertson (2000)
rules.quote: take a back seat to mouse clicks and momentum
rules.note: Extreme valuation with strong momentum stands for a market driven by momentum over value; Robertson exited months before the 2000 top, so timing may fail at 12 months.
rules.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Quote fragment verbatim in the letter; translation fair with timing caveat.

rules.principle: Size by recent volatility (N) because recent volatility predicts near-future volatility.
rules.source_title: Hackernoon, Huobi Quant Academy (3): Turtle trading rules
rules.quote: each N represents 1% of the account equity
rules.note: The Turtles used 20-day true range; a 12-month realized volatility above 20% is a monthly analog. This tests the premise of N sizing, not the Turtle system.
rules.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Quote verbatim on Hackernoon; note states it tests the premise, not the system.

rules.principle: Volatility-scaled sizing assumes high volatility is not paid for with higher return, so cutting size in volatile periods costs little.
rules.source_title: Hackernoon, Huobi Quant Academy (3): Turtle trading rules
rules.note: Loose: the Turtle rules imply equal risk per trade, not a return forecast; the test checks whether high-volatility months reward holders enough to justify full size.
rules.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Page supports equal-risk volatility sizing; looseness disclosed; no quote given.

rules.principle: Enter on breakouts to new highs, since a market at its highs is in a trend that tends to continue.
rules.source_title: The Investor's Podcast, Book review of Market Wizards
rules.quote: The market being in a trend is the main thing that eventually gets us in a trade.
rules.note: Loose: Turtle breakouts were 20- and 55-day highs; within 2% of the prior real peak with positive momentum is the nearest monthly analog of a breakout.
rules.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Dennis quote verbatim on The Investor's Podcast; looseness disclosed.

rules.principle: Do not get caught where you can lose a great deal: high volatility in a downtrend is where large losses come from.
rules.source_title: Antoine Buteau, Lessons from Bruce Kovner
rules.note: Kovner's rule is about position structure; reading it as avoiding volatile downtrends at index level is loose but testable.
rules.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Page has 'don't get caught in a situation in which you can lose a great deal of money'; looseness disclosed.

rules.principle: Balance must be built across inflation regimes because bonds and stocks fall together when inflation is high.
rules.source_title: Bridgewater Associates, The All Weather Story (Jan 2012)
rules.quote: The key was to put equal risk on each scenario to achieve balance.
rules.note: All Weather balances growth and inflation scenarios rather than forecasting; 12-month inflation above 4% marks the rising-inflation regime in which Treasuries are least likely to hedge equities, which bears directly on the TLT hedge.
rules.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Quote verbatim; page states rising inflation hurts both stocks and nominal bonds, so the inflation-regime test is fair.

rules.principle: Tail losses scale with current volatility on top of a heavy GPD tail, so the chance of a large fall is higher when recent volatility is high.
rules.source_title: McNeil and Frey, Estimation of tail-related risk measures for heteroscedastic financial time series (2000)
rules.quote: models with normally distributed conditional return distribution yield very bad estimates of the expected shortfall
rules.note: Conditional EVT says the tail quantile is sigma_t times a fixed GPD quantile; vol12 stands in for sigma_t and crash12 for a tail exceedance. Fair, with vol12 a slow proxy for monthly GARCH sigma.
rules.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Quote is verbatim on the McNeil-Frey page; conditional quantile = sigma_t times residual quantile supports the principle; vol12 proxy noted.

rules.principle: Because conditional tail loss is volatility times a fixed heavy-tailed quantile, the worst drawdown over the next year is deeper after high-volatility years.
rules.source_title: McNeil and Frey, Estimation of tail-related risk measures for heteroscedastic financial time series (2000)
rules.note: maxdd12 is negative, so lower means deeper. Same translation as the crash rule, scored on magnitude rather than frequency.
rules.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Same McNeil-Frey support; translation to deeper maxdd12 after high vol is fair and the note says so.

rules.principle: Experience rating holds that a risk's own recent loss experience carries predictive weight for its next period, so a market's own recent volatility should predict its next-year volatility.
rules.source_title: Buhlmann, Experience Rating and Credibility, ASTIN Bulletin 4(3), 1967
rules.quote: But is there a way to drop the condition of homogeneity (identical distribution)?
rules.note: Experience rating is about loss frequency and size, not volatility; the translation treats realized vol as the risk's loss experience. Expected to pass because of volatility clustering, so it calibrates how much credibility vol12 deserves.
rules.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Quote is verbatim in the RePEc abstract; the note flags that treating volatility as loss experience is loose.

rules.principle: Subject experience has predictive value that should be blended with relevant experience, so a negative stock-bond correlation over the past 36 months should make a negative correlation over the next 36 months more likely.
rules.source_title: Actuarial Standards Board, ASOP No. 25 Credibility Procedures
rules.quote: A measure of the predictive value in a given application that the actuary attaches to a particular set of data
rules.note: Direct experience-rating translation: past correlation is the subject experience, the 156-year base rate is the complement. Fair; the test measures how credible corr36 is for the Treasury hedge decision.
rules.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Quote is verbatim ASOP 25 sec 2.1; blending subject with relevant experience is sec 3.2; translation is fair.

rules.person: Davison and Smith (mean excess of the GPD)
rules.principle: Under a heavy GPD tail the expected overshoot beyond a threshold grows with the threshold, so once a market is already deep in loss, further losses are larger on average.
rules.source_title: VGAM documentation: meplot, Mean Excess Plot (Davison and Smith, 1990)
rules.quote: a diagnostic plot for the generalized Pareto distribution (GPD)
rules.note: Loose: the mean excess property applies to iid exceedances, while drawdown is a path statistic with mean reversion. Likely to fail if bear-market bottoms rebound, which is itself informative.
rules.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Quote is verbatim on the VGAM page; for xi > 0 the mean excess rises with u (slope xi/(1-xi)); note flags the iid-vs-path looseness.

rules.person: European Parliament and Council (Solvency II Article 106)
rules.principle: The equity capital charge is raised when the equity index stands above its weighted average level, implying equity risk is higher after strong rallies.
rules.source_title: Solvency II Directive, Article 106 (EIOPA rulebook)
rules.quote: shall be based on a function of the current level of an appropriate equity index
rules.note: Loose: the directive uses a 36-month average and the engine's trend_gap uses 10 months; the rule's stated aim is countercyclical capital, not a return forecast. Likely to fail because of momentum.
rules.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Quote is verbatim Article 106(2); note flags the 36 vs 10 month mismatch and that the rule sets capital, not a forecast.

rules.person: European Parliament and Council (Solvency II Article 106)
rules.principle: The equity capital charge is lowered after an index falls below its weighted average level, implying the regulator expects equity risk per unit held to be lower after a fall.
rules.source_title: Solvency II Directive, Article 106 (EIOPA rulebook)
rules.note: Loose: the article sets capital, not expected return; the translation reads a lower charge after falls as a higher reward per unit of risk. The 25% threshold is a round number for a deep fall.
rules.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Article 106 lowers the charge when the index is below its weighted average; note flags the loose reading as expected reward.

rules.person: Embrechts and Veraverbeke (via Asmussen and Binswanger)
rules.principle: With heavy-tailed losses a positive drift does not make ruin exponentially unlikely, because ruin comes from one large loss, so a positive trend should not protect against crashes in a high-volatility market.
rules.source_title: Asmussen and Binswanger, Simulation of Ruin Probabilities for Subexponential Claims, ASTIN Bulletin 27(2), 1997
rules.note: Loose: positive momentum plays the safety loading and high vol the heavy tail. A pass says trend does not cancel high-vol crash risk; a fail supports trend filters.
rules.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Asmussen and Binswanger say for subexponential claims only the largest claim causes ruin and R does not exist; note flags the momentum-as-loading looseness.

rules.principle: Extreme recent experience is partly noise and the best estimate shrinks toward the collective mean, so very high trailing earnings growth overstates the future and should precede lower returns.
rules.source_title: Efron and Morris, Data Analysis Using Stein's Estimator and Its Generalizations, JASA 70(350), 1975
rules.quote: shrinking all Xi toward X, an idea suggested by Lindley
rules.note: Loose: shrinkage is about estimating a mean, not about returns; this assumes prices extrapolate extreme earnings growth. Likely to fail because 25% earnings growth is common in recoveries, when returns are strong.
rules.checked: confirmed by a second checker: Quote 'shrinking all Xi toward X, an idea suggested by Lindley' is verbatim; note flags that the return translation is loose.
